readerTitle: Blockbuster saw Netflix coming. Why didn't that save it?
caseNote: 실제 기업 (Blockbuster, Netflix) + 실제 이론 (Christensen의 혁신 기업의 딜레마) + 가상 적용 (지역 화물 운송사)
insight: 기존 강자가 무너지는 이유는 위협을 못 봐서가 아니라, 올바른 대응이 지금의 수익 구조를 깎아 먹기 때문에 끝까지 밀어붙이지 못해서다.
misconception: Blockbuster는 경영진이 오만해서 Netflix를 무시했기 때문에 망했다.

sources.text: Randolph, M. (2019). That Will Never Work: The Birth of Netflix. 2000년 댈러스 회동과 5,000만 달러 인수 제안, 당시 Netflix의 적자
Antioco, J. (2011). How I Did It: Blockbuster's Former CEO on Sparring with an Activist Shareholder. Harvard Business Review, April 2011
Blockbuster의 Chapter 11 파산 신청 보도 (2010년 9월, 주요 언론)
Netflix 회사 연혁 및 투자자 자료 (1997년 설립, 2007년 스트리밍 시작, 2011년 Qwikster 발표와 철회)
Christensen, C. (1997). The Innovator's Dilemma. Harvard Business School Press

factChecks.note: 2000년 Netflix 공동창업자들이 댈러스에서 Blockbuster CEO John Antioco를 만나 5,000만 달러에 인수를 제안했고 거절당했다는 내용은 Randolph(2019)와 다수 보도에 나옵니다. '비웃었다'는 묘사는 일화성이라 카드에 쓰지 않았습니다.
연체료가 Blockbuster 수익의 상당 부분이었다는 점은 널리 보도됐지만 정확한 금액과 비중은 자료마다 다릅니다. 카드에는 수치 없이 'a meaningful slice'로만 적었습니다.
Blockbuster Online 출시(2004), 연체료 폐지('End of Late Fees', 2005년 1월), Total Access 출시(2006년 11월) 연도를 게시 전에 다시 확인하세요.
Antioco의 2007년 퇴임과 Carl Icahn과의 갈등, 후임 Jim Keyes가 매장 중심으로 방향을 돌린 점은 Antioco(HBR 2011)와 당시 보도로 확인하세요. 카드에는 후임자 이름을 쓰지 않았습니다.
Netflix 스트리밍 시작(2007년 1월), Blockbuster 파산 신청(2010년 9월), Qwikster 발표(2011년 9월)와 몇 주 뒤 철회(2011년 10월)를 확인하세요.
'thousands of stores'는 2000년대 중반 매장 수(약 9,000개로 자주 인용)를 수치 없이 표현한 것입니다.

cards.title: Blockbuster saw Netflix coming. Why didn't that save it?
body: In 2000, the founders of a small DVD-by-mail company flew to Dallas to meet the CEO of Blockbuster, the biggest video rental chain in the US.
Their offer: buy Netflix for $50 million and let it run Blockbuster's online business. Blockbuster said no. Ten years later, Blockbuster filed for bankruptcy.

image.label: A big video store beside a tiny mail envelope
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 왼쪽에 크고 화려한 비디오 대여 매장, 오른쪽에 작은 빨간 우편 봉투 하나가 매장 쪽으로 다가오는 모습. 실제 Blockbuster·Netflix 로고, 상표 색 조합, 간판 글씨는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: It's 2000. You run Blockbuster.
body: You have thousands of stores. On Friday night, customers walk in and leave with a new release. Late fees are a meaningful slice of your income.
Netflix mails DVDs, so customers wait days for a film. It is small and losing money. What do you do with the $50 million offer?

options.text: Buy it and run it as your online arm
options.feedback: You get a head start online. But you pay for a money-losing business whose main pitch, no late fees, attacks one of your own profit sources.

options.text: Decline, and build your own online service if demand grows
options.feedback: Cheaper, and it keeps options open. The risk is that "if demand grows" arrives later than you think, and building it means competing with your own stores.

options.text: Decline. Mail-order rental is a niche
options.feedback: Accurate in 2000. Most customers wanted a film tonight, not in three days. The real question is whether the niche stays a niche.

choice.afterReveal: Blockbuster declined. With what anyone knew in 2000, that looked like a sensible call.

cards.title: A worse product, for a different customer
body: Netflix was worse at what Blockbuster's best customers valued: a film tonight. It was better at things others cared about: no due dates, no late fees, a huge catalog delivered home.

This is how **disruptive innovation** usually starts. A newcomer serves customers the leader doesn't prize, with a product the leader's best customers would reject. Then it improves. By the time it's good enough for everyone, the leader's model is built for the old game.

image.label: Two customers: one wants tonight, one wants no late fees
image.brief: 두 명의 고객 일러스트. 왼쪽 고객 말풍선 "A film tonight", 오른쪽 고객 말풍선 "No due dates, no late fees". 오른쪽 아래에 작은 상승 화살표로 우편 서비스가 점점 좋아지는 모습. 로고 없음.

cards.title: Blockbuster did fight back.
body: The popular story is that Blockbuster ignored Netflix. It didn't. It launched Blockbuster Online in 2004, dropped late fees in 2005, and in 2006 launched Total Access, which let customers return mail DVDs at stores.

Each move cost money. Dropping late fees gave up income the stores relied on. Running mail rentals while paying for thousands of stores meant carrying two cost structures at once. This is the **innovator's dilemma**: the right move for the future makes this year's numbers look worse.
cards.softwareNote: A software company that earns heavily from overage charges or per-seat fees faces the same trap when a rival offers flat, simple pricing. Matching it is the right move and an instant hit to revenue.

cards.title: How it unwound
body: In 2007, CEO John Antioco left after a clash with activist investor Carl Icahn, partly over what these moves were costing. The new leadership turned back toward the stores. That same year, Netflix began streaming.

breakdown.label: Blockbuster responds
breakdown.detail: Online rentals, no late fees, Total Access

cards.title: Don't read this with hindsight.
body: Buying Netflix in 2000 would not have guaranteed anything. A store company could easily have starved or smothered it.
Netflix stumbled too. In 2011 it announced plans to split its DVD business into a separate service called Qwikster, then reversed within weeks after customer backlash.
The lesson isn't "always buy the upstart." It's that a response only works if you accept that it will hurt your current business for a while.

cards.title: Now it's a trucking company.
body: You run a regional freight firm with depots and your own fleet. Large shippers pay you well, and rush and after-hours surcharges add a healthy share of profit.
An upstart app matches small shippers with independent truckers. It's cheaper with no surcharges, but less predictable. Your big customers don't use it. Yet. What do you do?

options.text: Ignore it. Your best customers don't care
options.feedback: True today, and exactly how the 2000 view of Netflix looked. You save effort now but give the upstart years to improve unopposed.

options.text: Launch a small, separate service with its own targets, allowed to drop surcharges
options.feedback: You learn the new model and accept that it competes with your surcharges. Keeping it separate stops it from being judged by the core business's margins.

options.text: Add an app to your core business, keeping your usual pricing and surcharges
options.feedback: You look modern, but you keep the very fees that make the upstart attractive. Customers see the old deal in a new wrapper.

cards.title: Seeing the threat is easy. Paying for the response is hard.
body: Blockbuster saw Netflix and even copied it. What it couldn't sustain was letting the new model eat into the old profits.
**Try it today:** list where your profit really comes from. Then ask which of those sources a newcomer would happily give away.
